Re: the AI industry's focus existential threats.

item.title: I place different weights on things that might happen and things that definitely are happening. One thing that bugs me about existential-risk debates is that history is full of people at the forefront of genuinely important ideas who could not tell the difference between “this is a very big deal” and “this is the end of everything.”
item.description:
I place different weights on things that might happen and things that definitely are happening. One thing that bugs me about existential-risk debates is that history is full of people at the forefront of genuinely important ideas who could not tell the difference between “this is a very big deal” and “this is the end of everything.”

AI may pose existential risks. But it has already enabled an enormous transfer of value and power away from the people whose work made these systems possible. 

Too easy to let a possible future tragedy eclipse current harms. Too easy to think "WE ARE BECOME DEATH" because that feels horrifying but also kinda awesome. 

It's important to focus on reality because otherwise the odds that you end up in a cult get really high!

item.title: @hankgreen @technollama How would you prioritize these concerns? I think a lot of members of the AI industry feel pretty detached from the content creator debate over data harvesting because there are such massive existential risks posed by AI that data feels like the wrong issue to unite behind.
item.description: @hankgreen @technollama How would you prioritize these concerns? I think a lot of members of the AI industry feel pretty detached from the content creator debate over data harvesting because there are such massive existential risks posed by AI that data feels like the wrong issue to unite behind.

item.title: Vacuuming up extremely valuable training data that they will only compensate people for in specific circumstances where the stakeholders are powerful enough is one of my big concerns. But you’re right that it isn’t my only one.
item.description:
Vacuuming up extremely valuable training data that they will only compensate people for in specific circumstances where the stakeholders are powerful enough is one of my big concerns. But you’re right that it isn’t my only one.

I also think a lot of people at the major labs are correct that all of this would be much less dangerous if it weren’t happening so quickly. Rapid technological change tends to create asymmetric gains and losses, which tend to create social instability.

item.title: @hankgreen @technollama If the AI labs created an algorithm that didn’t require training data at all in order to create novel content, would you be against that?

items.title: I don't know why X has made it so hard for people to see alt tags but...here was the alt tag:
items.description:
I don't know why X has made it so hard for people to see alt tags but...here was the alt tag:

Somebody saying that daylight looked different in 2001, which is super fucking dumb. Daylight differs from day to day, obviously, but people seem increasingly anchored to the feeling that something has gone cosmologically wrong…that the light, the seasons, time itself, reality itself, all used to feel different. This is not new. It often intensifies during media revolutions, when the way we record the world changes, but also when the systems through which we share information begin selecting hypersalience over credibility. The strangest, most emotionally legible explanation wins distribution, which feels, to our minds, like evidence.
